identity.real_world_identity_notes: The McLaren F1 LM is the 1996 road-legal, limited-production Le Mans commemorative variant of the McLaren F1. McLaren built five customer cars, plus the XP LM prototype retained by McLaren. It is derived from the 1995 F1 GTR concept and uses GTR-derived race hardware, but it is not itself a 1995, 1996, or 1997 F1 GTR race car and must not inherit those cars' sequential or race-only controls.

McLaren's own heritage material identifies the LM as a five-car specification made in honour of the 1995 F1 GTR victory; BMW's heritage release separates the five LMs from the 28 GTR race cars; the exact-year production timing and GTR-derived LM specification are corroborated by the specialist technical history and the period MotorTrend test, which labels the car a 1996 F1 LM.

claims.basis: McLaren's own heritage material identifies the LM as a five-car specification made in honour of the 1995 F1 GTR victory; BMW's heritage release separates the five LMs from the 28 GTR race cars; the exact-year production timing and GTR-derived LM specification are corroborated by the specialist technical history and the period MotorTrend test, which labels the car a 1996 F1 LM.

The exact LM specification says six-speed, the period test says 6-speed manual, and the specialist history says GTR-sourced six-speed manual. The exact LM specification explicitly says 'All synchro constant mesh'; Road & Track independently describes the F1/Weismann family as using BMW synchronizers. The LM sheet's separate 'straight cut gears' line describes gear-tooth form, not a dogbox claim, so it is not treated as a conflict. The period test and specialist history establish a manual gear lever, the interior photograph shows a gated central lever, and the community evidence explicitly identifies the road-car LM gate as standard gated. The confidence remains low because no factory gate drawing was found. The only source that names the pattern calls the F1 LM road-car gate standard gated; the photograph corroborates a gated manual selector but does not show a full diagram. The specialist description calls it a suede-rimmed GTR steering wheel, and the CC-licensed interior photograph visibly shows a continuous circular three-spoke rim. The high-resolution interior photograph visibly shows rim material joining the left and right grips across the top, so the rim is not open-top. The reviewed sources did not establish the remaining technique and wheel fields, which stay unknown in the real-car baseline: /authentic_controls/transmission/first_gear_position, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/standing_start_clutch, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/integrated_display, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shift_lights.
Directly observed during the guided drive: move-off, shift clutch use, automatic cut and blip, and the cockpit rim.

driver_summary: Six-speed synchromesh in the road-legal LM, of which McLaren built five customer cars. No source establishes its technique, and Assetto Corsa wants a blip on the way down: that is the simulator's demand rather than a requirement of the gearbox.
